newsitem.title: UK: Children sing for N.Irish peace as hopes fade.
newsitem.headline: Children sing for N.Irish peace as hopes fade.

text.p: Hundreds of Protestant and Catholic youngsters gathered in biting cold in central Belfast on Sunday to sing Christmas carols for a peace that many people in Northern Ireland think might be ebbing away.
An hour later, a car bomb exploded and badly injured a Catholic man, raising fears that the British province might be edging towards a new flareup of sectarian violence.
No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack but Irish republicans said they believed it was the work of pro-British Loyalist guerrillas.

The carol-singers met at the spot where U.S. President Bill Clinton stood in the run-up to last Christmas. But the peace fervour he promoted on a short trip to the partitioned island has now dissipated.
The car bomb, which wounded a well-known republican, followed an IRA shooting attack that caused outrage across the sectarian divide.

"The atmosphere is bad," said one Protestant Loyalist politician hours after Irish Republican Army gunmen opened fire at policemen inside a children's hospital late on Friday, slightly injuring one of them.

Two IRA men disguised as visitors walked up a corridor in the Belfast hospital and shot at policemen acting as bodyguards for a Protestant politician who was at the bedside of his seriously ill seven-year-old son.
On the streets of Belfast, people were fearful.

"When you take to shooting people in a children's hospital and try to shoot a man whose child is very ill, I don't think there's a lot of hope for this country," said one anquished woman at the carol service.

"I'm a doctor and I've seen families ruined, lives ruined, people injured and people dead. There's no need for it. Things can be achieved without violence," she added, her teenage daughter by her side.
A Protestant man on his way to church said the outlook was bleak. "Things are at the white-knuckle stage," he said.
A Catholic with his young son on his shoulders to see the carol-singers praised for Loyalist politicians who had tried to persuade their guerrilla allies to abide by a two-year truce.

"I think the peace process has gone too far to go back. I believe that while there will be some kind of a breakdown in the cessation of violence, that people will go back to the peace process," he said.

A leader of one of the banned Loyalist groups, so-called for their loyalty to Britain, told The Sunday Times that his men were tired of being lauded for their patience in the face of what they see as provocation by IRA fighters.
"There will definitely be a response to this," said the man, a member of the banned Ulster Defence Association.

The IRA, which is fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland, ended a 17-month truce last February with a bomb attack in London and has since set off several more bombs, mainly on mainland Britain.
Britain and Ireland insist that the IRA must renew the ceasefire before Sinn Fein, its political wing, can take part in peace talks.
